newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Soyinka, 11 dissidents face Nigeria treason charge.
newsitem.headline: Soyinka, 11 dissidents face Nigeria treason charge.

text.p: Exiled Nobel laureate Wole Soyinka and 11 other dissidents on Wednesday were charged with treason by Nigeria's military government over a spate of recent bomb blasts in the country.
They face the death penalty if convicted.

Along with Soyinka, others charged in absentia at a magistrate court in the Ikeja district of Lagos were some exiled leaders of the opposition group NADECO, including former army chief Lieutenant-General Alani Akinrinade and war time information minister Anthony Enahoro.
Eight of the dissidents are in the country and were brought to court, court officials. The case was adjourned to May 9.
The case comes up just days before Nigeria holds the first multi-party poll since the annulment of a 1993 vote that was meant to restore democracy.

Political sources said they did not expect the case to affect the local council poll scheduled for Saturday in which five recently registered political parties would be vying to run town halls in more than a thousand local councils nationwide.
Soyinka and some of those charged with him have campaigned to have the annulled poll recognised as legitimate and its presumed winner businessman Moshood Abiola installed president.
Soyinka and many opposition figures fled Nigeria two years ago to Europe and the United States, where they have campaigned against the military government of General Sani Abacha.
Political sources said charging them could pave the way for Nigeria to try to get them extradited back home.
The accused face a two count charge of "conspiracy to levy war against the federal military government of Nigeria" and "causing explosions in various parts of Nigeria."
Others on the charge sheet Frederick Fasehun, president of the Campaign for Democracy pressure group as well as former finance minister Olu Falae.
The last two have been detained since December after a spate of bomb explosions hit army buses, killing at least three soldiers and wounding several dozens.
A Lagos high court judge on Wednesday ordered that Fasehun be released.
Charging him formally before a magistrate court now makes his release unlikely because capital offences are not bailable.
Police have publicly blamed Soyinka and NADECO for the bombs and while both have denied any involvement, Soyinka refused in an interview with BBC radio to condemn the bombings.

The men will be defended by Gani Fawehinmi, one of two radical opposition lawyers recently released from detention who have offered free legal services to Abiola, who is also facing treason charges and has been held since 1994 when he proclaimed himself president.
The annulment of the 1993 poll plunged Africa's most populous nation into political crisis.
Abacha, who seized power in the chaos that followed is implementing a transition plan he says will see him hand power to a democratically-elected president in October 1998.
But his critics dismiss the transition programme, saying he intends to use it to retain power.
His government has been subjected to several investigations over alleged human rights abuses, the latest being the current visit of a team from the Gambia-based African rights commission.
The mission, led by Ghanaian professor Victor Danqua was turned away on Wednesday when it went to meet the Civil Liberties Organisation, the leading rights group in Nigeria.
Local rights activists deride the team as not objective because it is visiting after a United Nations team called off a similar mission because it was denied access to jails and detainees.
